questions.question: If the distance between object and its two times magnified virtual image produced by a curved mirror is $15\mathrm{cm}$, the focal length of the mirror must be :
questions.explanation: Let object be at a distance $x\mathrm{cm}$ from the pole. Then, distance of image from the pole will be $= 15 - x$. Given: Magnification, $m = 2 = \frac{ - v}{u} \implies 2 = \frac{ - (15 - x)}{ - x} \implies 2x = 15 - x \implies 3x = 15\;$ Now, Distance of the image from the pole $= 15 - x = 15 - 5 = 10\mathrm{cm}$ Therefore, $v = 10\mathrm{cm}$ From mirror formula: $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{( - 5)} = \frac{1 - 2}{10} = \frac{ - 1}{10} \implies f = - 10\mathrm{cm}$ !

questions.question: The driver sitting inside a parked car is watching vehicles approaching from behind with the help of his side view mirror, which is a convex mirror with radius of curvature $\mathrm{R}=2 \mathrm{~m}$. Another car approaches him from behind with a uniform speed of $90 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{hr}$. When the car is at a distance of 24 m from him, the magnitude of the acceleration of the image of the car in the side view mirror is ' a '. The value of 100 a is _______ $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}^2$.
questions.explanation:
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{v}=\frac{\mathrm{uf}}{\mathrm{u}-\mathrm{f}}=\frac{-24 \cdot 1}{-24-1}=\frac{24}{25} \\ & \mathrm{~m}=\frac{-\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{u}}=-\frac{24}{25(-24)}=\frac{1}{25} \\ & \frac{1}{\mathrm{v}}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{u}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}} \\ & \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{I}}=-\mathrm{m}^2 \cdot \mathrm{v}_0=\frac{-1}{(25)^2} \cdot 25=\frac{-1}{25} \end{aligned}$

Diff. $\begin{aligned} & \frac{-1}{\mathrm{v}^2}\left(\frac{\mathrm{dv}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right)+\frac{1}{\mathrm{u}^2}\left(\frac{\mathrm{du}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right)=0\left[\frac{\mathrm{dv}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{i}} ; \frac{\mathrm{du}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\mathrm{v}_0\right] \\ & \frac{+2}{\mathrm{v}^3} \cdot\left(\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{t}}\right)^2-\frac{1}{\mathrm{v}^2} \cdot \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{L}}-\frac{2}{\mathrm{u}^3} \cdot\left(\mathrm{v}_0\right)^2+\frac{1}{\mathrm{u}^2} \cdot \mathrm{a}_0=0 \\ & \frac{\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{I}}}{\mathrm{v}^2}=\frac{2}{\mathrm{v}^3} \cdot \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{I}}^2-\frac{2}{\mathrm{u}^3} \cdot \mathrm{v}_0^2 \\ & \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{I}}=\frac{2}{\mathrm{v}} \cdot \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{I}}^2-\frac{2 \mathrm{v}^2}{\mathrm{u}^3} \cdot \mathrm{v}_0^2 \\ & =\frac{2 \cdot 25}{24} \cdot \frac{1}{25} \cdot \frac{1}{25}-\frac{2}{(24)^3} \cdot \frac{24}{25} \cdot \frac{24}{25} \cdot 25 \cdot 25 \\ & \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{I}}=\frac{2}{24.25}-\frac{2}{24} \\ & \mathrm{a}_1=\frac{2}{24} \cdot \frac{-24}{25}=\frac{-2}{25} \\ & 100 a_1=\frac{2}{25} \times 100=8 \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation: Let's consider the following diagram- Let's assume that ${v}_{A},{v}_{B}$ indicates the distances of the images of objects A and B respectively. Thus, by mirror formula, for object A, it can be written that $\begin{matrix}\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} & = & \frac{1}{f} \\ \frac{1}{{v}_{A}} + \frac{1}{ - 15} & = & \frac{1}{\left( - 20\right)} \\ \frac{1}{{v}_{A}} & = & \frac{1}{ - 20} + \frac{1}{15} \\ = \frac{ - 3 + 4}{60} \\ {v}_{A} & = & 60\mathrm{cm}\end{matrix}$ Similarly, for object B, using mirror formula, $\begin{matrix}\frac{1}{{v}_{B}} + \frac{1}{\left( - 25\right)} & = & \frac{1}{\left( - 20\right)} \\ \frac{1}{{v}_{B}} & = & \frac{ - 1}{20} + \frac{1}{25} \\ & = & \frac{ - 5 + 4}{100} \\ & = & \frac{ - 1}{100} \\ {v}_{B} & = & - 100cm\end{matrix}$ Hence, the distance $\left(d\right)$ between the images can be calculated as follows: $\begin{matrix}d & = & {v}_{A} + {v}_{B} \\ & = & \left(60 + 100\right)\mathrm{cm} \\ & = & 160\mathrm{cm}\end{matrix}$

questions.question: In an experiment for estimating the value of focal length of converging mirror, image of an object placed at $40\mathrm{cm}$ from the pole of the mirror is formed at distance $120\mathrm{cm}$ from the pole of the mirror. These distances are measured with a modified scale in which there are $20$ small divisions in $1\mathrm{cm}$. The value of error in measurement of focal length of the mirror is $\frac{1}{K}\mathrm{cm}$. The value of $K$ is ______.
questions.explanation:
Given here, $u = - 40\mathrm{cm},v = - 120\mathrm{cm}$

Using mirror formula, $\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \frac{ - 1}{120} - \frac{1}{40} = \frac{1}{f}\;$

Now, differentiating mirror equation, we get

$\frac{ - 1}{{v}^{2}}dv - \frac{1}{{u}^{2}}du = - \frac{1}{{f}^{2}}df$

Also, the least count of scale, $dv = du = \frac{1}{20}\mathrm{cm}$

Putting in above equation,

$∴\frac{\frac{1}{20}}{(120{)}^{2}} + \frac{\frac{1}{20}}{(40{)}^{2}} = \frac{df}{(30{)}^{2}}$

On solving, we get

$df = \frac{1}{32}\mathrm{cm} ∴K = 32$.

questions.question:
A light wave travelling linearly in a medium of dielectric constant $4$, incidents on the horizontal interface separating medium with air. The angle of incidence for which the total intensity of incident wave will be reflected back into the same medium will be :

(Given : relative permeability of medium ${\mu }_{r} = 1$)
questions.explanation:
Relative refractive index is $\mu = \sqrt{{\mu }_{r}{\epsilon }_{r}} = \sqrt{4 \times 1} = 2$

Now, for complete reflection, $\theta > {\theta }_{c}$, where, ${\theta }_{c}$ is critical angle.

Now, critical angle is $\sin {\theta }_{c} = \frac{1}{\mu } = \frac{1}{2} \implies {\theta }_{c} = {\sin }^{ - 1}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\;$

So, the angle of incidence for which the total intensity of incident wave will be reflected back into the same medium is $\theta > 30 ^\circ$ i.e., $60 ^\circ$.

questions.question: Time taken by light to travel in two different materials $A$ and $B$ of refractive indices ${\mu }_{A}$ and ${\mu }_{B}$ of same thickness is ${t}_{1}$ and ${t}_{2}$ respectively. If ${t}_{2} - {t}_{1} = 5 \times {10}^{ - 10}s$ and the ratio of ${\mu }_{A}$ to ${\mu }_{B}$ is $1 : 2$. Then the thickness of material, in meter is: (Given ${v}_{A}$ and ${v}_{B}$ are velocities of light in $A$ and $B$ materials respectively).
questions.explanation:
The speed of light in a medium is inversely proportional to the refractive index of the material. Therefore,

$\frac{{\mu }_{A}}{{\mu }_{B}} = \frac{{v}_{B}}{{v}_{A}} = \frac{1}{2}$

Let the thickness is $d \implies {t}_{2} - {t}_{1} = \frac{d}{{v}_{B}} - \frac{d}{{v}_{A}} = 5 \times {10}^{ - 10}s$

As ${v}_{A} = 2{v}_{B} \implies d = 5 \times {10}^{ - 10} \times 2{v}_{B} \implies d = 5 \times {10}^{ - 10} \times {v}_{A}m$.

questions.question: A monochromatic light wave with wavelength ${\lambda }_{1}$ and frequency ${\nu }_{1}$ in air enters another medium. If the angle of incidence and angle of refraction at the interface are $45 ^\circ$ and $30 ^\circ$ respectively, then the wavelength ${\lambda }_{2}$ and frequency ${\nu }_{2}$ of the refracted wave are:
questions.explanation:
By using Snell's law, ${n}_{1}\sin {\theta }_{1} = {n}_{2}\sin {\theta }_{2}$, the refractive index is

$\mu = \frac{\sin 45 ^\circ }{\sin 30 ^\circ } = \frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}{\frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{2}$

Also using the relation $n = \frac{c}{v}$ where $n$ is the refractive index, $c$ is the velocity of light in air and $v$ is the velocity in the medium

$\implies \frac{{c}_{\text{air }}}{\text{v}\text{ }} = \sqrt{2} = \frac{{\lambda }_{\text{1 }}}{{\lambda }_{2}}$

The velocities are given by

$v = \nu {\lambda }_{2}\; \implies {\lambda }_{1} = \sqrt{2}{\lambda }_{2}$ and ${\nu }_{1} = {\nu }_{2}$.

The frequency of light does not change when the medium changes.

questions.question: The critical angle for a denser-rarer interface is $45 ^\circ$. The speed of light in rarer medium is $3 \times {10}^{8}m{s}^{ - 1}$. The speed of light in the denser medium is:
questions.explanation:
The critical angle and the refractive index of a media are related by the formula:

$\sin {\theta }_{c} = \left(\frac{1}{\mu }\right)...\left(1\right)$

Substitute the value of the critical angle into equation (1) and solve to calculate the refractive index of the medium.

$\begin{matrix}\sin 45 ^\circ & = & \frac{1}{\mu } \\ \implies \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\mu } \\ \implies \mu = \sqrt{2}\end{matrix}$

The refractive index of the medium can also be written as

$\mu = \frac{c}{v}...\left(2\right)$

Substitute the values of the known parameters into equation (2) and solve to calculate the required speed of light within the medium.

$\begin{matrix}\sqrt{2} & = & \frac{3 \times {10}^{8}m{s}^{ - 1}}{v} \\ \implies v = \frac{3 \times {10}^{8}m{s}^{ - 1}}{\sqrt{2}} \\ = 2.12 \times {10}^{8}m{s}^{ - 1}\end{matrix}$

Given below are two statements: one is labelled as **Assertion A** and the other is labelled as **Reason R**

**Assertion A:** The phase difference of two light waves change if they travel through different media having same thickness, but different indices of refraction.

**Reason R:** The wavelengths of waves are different in different media.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
options: Both **A** and **R** are correct but **R** is NOT the correct explanation of **A**
**A** is not correct but **R** is correct
**A** is correct but **R** is not correct
Both **A** and **R** are correct and **R** is the correct explanation of **A**
questions.explanation:
When light travels through a medium, its velocity depends on the density of the medium.

The formula to calculate the speed of light can be written as

$v = \nu \lambda ...(1)$

From equation (1), it can be concluded that higher the speed, higher is the wavelength. Hence, the wavelength of light depends on the refractive index of the medium.

Because of changed wavelength the phase difference changes while the two waves travel the same distance.

Thus, both **A** and **R** are correct and **R** is the correct explanation of **A**.

questions.question:
A convex lens of refractive index $1.5$ and focal length $18\mathrm{cm}$ in air is immersed in water. The change in focal length of the lens will be_____$\mathrm{cm}$.

(Given refractive index of water$= \frac{4}{3}$)
questions.explanation:
From Lens Maker's formula,

For air: $\frac{1}{{f}_{a}} = \left(\frac{{\mu }_{g}}{{\mu }_{a}} - 1\right)\left(\frac{1}{{R}_{1}} - \frac{1}{{R}_{2}}\right)$

For water: $\frac{1}{{f}_{w}} = \left(\frac{{\mu }_{g}}{{\mu }_{w}} - 1\right)\left(\frac{1}{{R}_{1}} - \frac{1}{{R}_{2}}\right) ∴\frac{\frac{1}{{f}_{a}}}{\frac{1}{{f}_{w}}} = \frac{\left(\frac{{\mu }_{g}}{{\mu }_{a}} - 1\right)}{\left(\frac{{\mu }_{g}}{{\mu }_{w}} - 1\right)} \implies \frac{{f}_{w}}{{f}_{a}} = \frac{\left(1.5 - 1\right)}{\left(\frac{1.5 \times 3}{4} - 1\right)} \implies {f}_{w} = \frac{0.5}{0.125} \times 18 = 72\mathrm{cm}$

Thus, change in focal length of the lens is $72 - 18 = 54\mathrm{cm}$

$\frac{1}{{f}_{a}} = \left({\mu }_{1} - 1\right)\left(\frac{2}{R}\right)$

$\frac{{f}_{m}}{{f}_{a}} = \frac{\left({\mu }_{1} - 1\right){\mu }_{m}}{\left({\mu }_{1} - {\mu }_{m}\right)}...\left(1\right)$

Equation (1) implies that

$\frac{{f}_{m}}{20} = \frac{(1.5 - 1)1.6}{(1.5 - 1.6)}\;$

velocity of image wrt. to lens is given by

\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{I} / \mathrm{L}}=\left(\frac{60 \times 1}{197 \times 20}\right)^{2}

\end{array}$$

questions.question: A bi convex lens of focal length $10\mathrm{cm}$ is cut in two identical parts along a plane perpendicular to the principal axis. The power of each lens after cut is _____ $D$.
questions.explanation:
The focal length of the bi-convex lens $\left(f\right)$ can be calculated as follows:

$\begin{matrix}\frac{1}{f} & = & (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R} - \frac{1}{ - R}\right) \\ & = & \frac{2\left(\mu - 1\right)}{R}...\left(1\right)\end{matrix}$

When the lens is cut into two halves, the focal length $\left(f'\right)$ of each part can be calculated as follows:

$\begin{matrix}\frac{1}{{f}^{'}} & = & (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R} - \frac{1}{ \infty }\right) \\ & = & \frac{\left(\mu - 1\right)}{R}...\left(2\right)\end{matrix}$

Hence, the ratio of the powers for both the lenses can be given by

$\begin{matrix}\frac{{P}^{'}}{P} & = & \frac{\frac{1}{f'}}{\frac{1}{f}} \\ & = & \frac{f}{f'} \\ & = & \frac{\frac{\left(\mu - 1\right)}{R}}{\frac{2\left(\mu - 1\right)}{R}} \\ & = & \frac{1}{2} \\ & \implies & P' = \frac{P}{2}...\left(3\right)\end{matrix}$

Substitute the value of the known parameter into equation (3) to calculate the required power.

$\begin{matrix}P' & = & \frac{10D}{2} \\ & = & 5D\end{matrix}$

,
